extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of 18th-century European diplomatic and political history; historians
extracted.subtask_description: A narrative and analytical account of the foreign-policy actions and character of the Marquis d'Argenson during 1745–1746, assessing diplomatic choices, causes of failure, and qualities of statesmanship. The text mixes chronological reportage with evaluative judgments about ministers, negotiations, and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministerial competence in court politics
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful minister needs aptitude for court intrigue and the power to confront and neutralise opposition; inability to manage courtiers or coerce political enemies undermines policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual basis: 'He had no aptitude for court intrigue; he had no power of confronting opposition and sternly frowning it down... Unable to win, he neglected the courtiers.' Examples/anti-patterns: neglecting court relations or refusing to engage in political management leads to isolation and eventual dismissal (as happened to d'Argenson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise national interest and long-term strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Statesmanship is judged by regard to the interest of the country and long-standing strategic tradition, not by short-term office-seeking or courting favourites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual basis: 'D'Argenson's statesmanship had a broader base. It had regard, not to the interest of his place or to the opinion of de Pompadour, but to the interest of his country and the tradition of Richelieu.' Guidance: weigh long-term geopolitical consequences over immediate court politics or transient popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure material means to back policy
rubrics_metrics.description: A policy that requires military or other tangible backing cannot be credibly pursued without the corresponding forces or resources; rhetoric alone is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual basis: 'he was unable, through no fault of his own, to give them the weight of a single cannon-shot... the bold policy of the 31st of January... was tacitly abandoned by the French Government.' Anti-pattern: proclaiming or negotiating substantive commitments while lacking armies or means to enforce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess strategic value of territories and long-term consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions should be guided by strategic evaluation (e.g., the relative value of Silesia, Alsace, Lorraine) and their wider European repercussions, not merely immediate gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual basis: d'Argenson's view that 'Silesia as strategically the most valuable of the French provinces' and his warning that if Frederick bowed, Austria would be strengthened. Guidance: evaluate how territorial outcomes reshape alliances and future balances of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand other actors' motives and material interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Diplomacy must not assume other governments share your motives; negotiators must account for rivals' and allies' immediate material interests and risk tolerances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual basis: 'He made a fatal mistake in attributing his own motives to the Sardinian Government... imagining that it would consent for a national ideal to hazard its present and material interests.' Anti-pattern: projection of one's motives leads to misreading partners and doomed negotiations (e.g., Turin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehend positions of all parties in multilateral negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful negotiations require a clear understanding of the aims and constraints of every party; failure often arises when 'not one of the parties... understood the position of the rest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual basis: description of the Negotiation of Turin as 'an intricate play of cross-purposes.' Practical guidance: map each actor's incentives, red lines, and domestic pressures before finalising agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisiveness and practical action over casuistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Statesmanship favors clear, decisive, and practical measures rather than fine ethical distinctions or hair-splitting legalism when timely action is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual basis: 'To Frederick, the difference between the open rupture of an alliance and the tacit abandonment of an ally, was one for a casuist and not for a statesman.' Guidance: when alliances or military realities shift, favour concrete measures that protect core interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain realistic expectations about allied cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not count on unconditional loyalty or consistent behaviour from allies; cultivate arrangements that tolerate shifting interests and keep options open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual basis: observations on Prussia's defection/neutrality and d'Argenson's suggestion to 'leave him alone; he will remain neutral... he will deceive the Queen of Hungary as he deceives everybody else.' Guidance: design policies that anticipate opportunism—seek understandings that constrain harm even when alliances fray.
